title: Application architecture
summary: Design how the pieces of an AI app fit together — frontend, backend, model API, and data — so it stays clean and scalable.
objectives: Explain what application architecture is and why it matters for portfolio projects
Identify the core layers: frontend, backend, model/API, and data store
Separate concerns so each layer has one clear responsibility
Understand the request flow from user click to model response and back
Keep secrets like API keys out of the frontend and in environment variables
Choose between monolith and simple service split for a small project
Draw a clear architecture diagram to include in your portfolio

quiz.q: In a typical AI web app, where should your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY live?
options: In the backend, read from an environment variable
quiz.why: The key must stay server-side in an env var. If it is in the frontend, anyone can read it from the browser and steal it.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of 'separation of concerns'?
options: It makes the app run faster
Each part has one job, so it is easier to change and test
It removes the need for a database
It hides the code from users
quiz.why: When each layer does one thing, you can change or fix one part without breaking the others, and you can test them independently.

quiz.q: Which layer is responsible for calling the Claude Messages API and shaping the prompt?
quiz.why: The backend holds the secret key and business logic, so it calls the model API. The frontend just sends user input and shows results.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what is application architecture?
quiz.answer: The high-level design of how an application's parts (frontend, backend, model, data) are split up and connected.
quiz.why: Architecture is the shape of the system — which components exist and how they talk — not the line-by-line code inside them.

quiz.q: Why might you start a small portfolio project as a monolith rather than many microservices?
quiz.answer: A monolith is simpler to build, deploy, and reason about; microservices add overhead you rarely need at small scale.
quiz.why: For a one-person portfolio project, a single deployable app is easier and faster; you split into services only when there is a real reason.

quiz.q: What does the backend act as between the user and the model API?
quiz.answer: A trusted middle layer (a proxy/gateway) that holds secrets, validates input, and forwards requests.
quiz.why: The backend shields the API key, controls what gets sent, and lets you add logging, limits, and error handling in one place.

body_markdown:
## What is application architecture?

**Application architecture** is the high-level design of how the parts of your app fit together. Not the line-by-line code — the *shape*. Which components exist, what each one does, and how they talk to each other.

For a portfolio AI app, getting this right means a recruiter can read your diagram and instantly understand your thinking. That clarity is worth as much as the code itself.

## The core layers

Most AI web apps have four layers:

- **Frontend** — what the user sees and clicks (the browser).
- **Backend** — your server code; holds secrets and business logic.
- **Model / API** — the Claude Messages API that does the A I work.
- **Data store** — a database or files where you keep state.

The golden rule is **separation of concerns**: each layer has *one* job. That makes the system easy to change, test, and explain.

## The request flow

Follow a single click through the system. The user types a question and presses send. The frontend sends that text to your backend. The backend validates it, attaches the secret key, and calls the model. The model replies, the backend cleans it up, and the frontend shows it.

The frontend never talks to the model directly. The backend is a **trusted middle layer**.

```python
# backend: app.py (Flask)
import os
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
from anthropic import Anthropic

app = Flask(__name__)
client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from env

@app.post("/ask")
def ask():
    user_text = request.json["question"]
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
        max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_text}],
    )
    return jsonify({"answer": msg.content[0].text})
```

## Keep secrets out of the frontend

Your `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is like a password. If it sits in browser code, anyone can open dev tools and steal it. Keep it on the **server**, loaded from an environment variable — never committed to Git.

```bash
# set the key in your shell or a .env file (gitignored)
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."

# .gitignore
.env
```

## Monolith vs services

For a small portfolio project, start with a **monolith** — one deployable app containing frontend and backend. It is simpler to build, deploy, and reason about. Split into separate services only when there is a real reason: different scaling needs, separate teams, or independent deploys. Do not add microservices just to look advanced.

## Your task

Draw the architecture diagram for one of your projects: boxes for each layer, arrows for the request flow, and a note on where the secret key lives. Add it to your README.

slides.title: Application architecture
slides.narration: Welcome back to Month Four, where we turn your skills into portfolio projects. In this lesson we step up from writing code to designing systems. We'll look at application architecture: how the pieces of an A I app fit together, and how to draw a clear picture of it that recruiters will love.

slides.title: What is architecture?
bullets: The high-level design of your app.
Which parts exist and how they connect.
The shape, not the line-by-line code.
A clear diagram shows your thinking.
slides.narration: So what do we mean by application architecture? It's the high-level design of your app: which components exist, what each one does, and how they talk to each other. It's the shape of the system, not the detailed code inside. A clear architecture diagram instantly shows a recruiter how you think.

slides.title: The four core layers
bullets: Frontend: what the user sees and clicks.
Backend: your server, holds the secrets.
Model API: Claude does the A I work.
Data store: where you keep state.
slides.narration: Most A I web apps have four layers. The frontend is what the user sees and clicks in the browser. The backend is your server code, which holds the secrets and the logic. The model A P I is where Claude does the actual A I work. And the data store is a database or files where you keep state. Four boxes, four jobs.

slides.title: Separation of concerns
bullets: Each layer has exactly one job.
Change one part without breaking others.
Test each layer on its own.
Easier to explain and extend.
slides.narration: The golden rule of good architecture is separation of concerns. Each layer should have exactly one job. When you keep them separate, you can change or fix one part without breaking the others, and you can test each piece on its own. It also makes your project much easier to explain and to grow later.

slides.title: The request flow
bullets: User clicks, frontend sends the text.
Backend validates and adds the key.
Backend calls the model, gets a reply.
Frontend shows the answer.
slides.narration: Let's follow a single click through the system. The user types a question and presses send. The frontend passes that text to your backend. The backend checks it, attaches the secret key, and calls the model. Claude replies, the backend tidies it up, and the frontend displays the answer. Clean and predictable.

slides.title: Backend is the middle layer
bullets: Frontend never calls the model directly.
Backend holds the key and the logic.
It is a trusted proxy or gateway.
One place for limits and logging.
slides.narration: Notice that the frontend never talks to the model directly. The backend sits in the middle as a trusted gateway. It holds the key, validates the input, and calls the messages create endpoint. Because everything funnels through one place, that's also where you add rate limits, logging, and error handling.

slides.title: Keep secrets server-side
bullets: The A P I key is like a password.
Never put it in frontend code.
Read it from an environment variable.
Never commit it to Git.
slides.narration: Your Anthropic A P I key is like a password. If it lives in browser code, anyone can open dev tools and steal it. So keep it on the server, loaded from an environment variable, and add your dot env file to gitignore. The client library reads the key automatically, so your code never has to print it.

slides.title: Monolith vs services
bullets: Start with a monolith: one app.
Simpler to build and deploy.
Split into services only when needed.
Don't add complexity to look clever.
slides.narration: For a small portfolio project, start with a monolith: a single app that holds your frontend and backend together. It's simpler to build, deploy, and reason about. Only split into separate services when there's a real reason, like different scaling needs. Resist adding microservices just to look advanced; simple wins.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Leaking the key into the frontend.
Mixing all layers into one tangle.
Over-engineering a tiny project.
No diagram in the README.
slides.narration: Let's flag the traps. One: leaking the A P I key into frontend code. Two: mixing every concern into one tangled file. Three: over-engineering a tiny project with services it doesn't need. And four: shipping a project with no architecture diagram. A simple, honest diagram beats a fancy, undocumented build every time.
